title: Participation ratio in lessons: the results are in!
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton reports the results of his participation-ratio survey, in which over 500 teachers rated student participation across five lesson phases, and uses them to diagnose where checking for understanding breaks down. For each phase he pairs the survey result with strategies from teachers who rated themselves High, then adds his own critique. His recurring move is to argue that circulation alone is not a reliable check for understanding in large classes and should be combined with whole-class mini-whiteboard responses. He flags the 10% of teachers who skip a prerequisite knowledge check as taking a risk, recommends diagnostic multiple-choice questions for that phase, and notes that the explanation and worked-example phase is both the most-chosen priority and his own weakest area. On plenaries, he argues they are unnecessary if checks run throughout the lesson, but that those done should assess core knowledge rather than an extension question. Much of the post is quoted teacher responses, but Barton's own commentary on each phase carries a clear formative-assessment argument.
points: Barton contends that circulation, the strategy most High-rating teachers cited, must be paired with something like a whole-class mini-whiteboard check to be reliable in large classes.
He recommends making the prerequisite knowledge check look different from the Do Now, using diagnostic questions, so students recognise it as a separate phase with its own purpose.
The explanation and worked-example phase was the one teachers most wanted to improve, and Barton admits it is where his own participation ratio is lowest.
During practice, he argues students tune out when the teacher goes through answers, and proposes a critical question answered on mini-whiteboards on a count of three.
A plenary, if used, should allow adequate time, involve the whole class and target the lesson's core knowledge rather than a final hard extension question.
quotes: This result echoes what I see a lot in the classrooms I visit. Often students are not engaged during the Do Now. Many are slow to settle, and when they do eventually settle they embark on an elaborate ploy of Busy Tricking, giving the impression they are thinking when in fact they are not.

Whilst I am a huge advocate of purposeful circulation (we will discuss this in a future newsletter), I think it needs to be combined with something like a whole-class mini-whiteboard check to get a reliable check for understanding, especially in classes with a large number of students.

An interesting thing to note here is the 10% of teachers who do not do a prerequisite knowledge check. Perhaps this is built into the Do Now. But if not, it feels risky to assume the foundations are secure enough to build a new idea upon.

Personally, I am a fan of ensuring the format of the prerequisite knowledge check is different to that used in the retrieval Do Now. I want students to see each as a separate phase of the lesson so they better appreciate the purpose. Also, mixing things up can be good to combat any declining attention.
This is no surprise. If we are not careful, it can be so easy for students to stop listening or thinking whilst the teacher offers an explanation or goes through a worked example.

Effective circulation can really help ensure students are putting effort into the practice. But it is when the teacher goes through the answers that I find some students tune out. To address this, I like to choose a critical question and ask all students to copy their final answer on their mini-whiteboards.

If regular checks for understanding have been present throughout the lesson, then there may not be any need for a formal plenary. However, if we are doing a plenary to get a sense of where the class is at, it is a good idea to allow adequate time, ensure whole-class participation, and pitch our questions carefully so that they assess the core knowledge of the lesson (as opposed to being an extension question that only a few students can access).
